paper_core_claims.claim: A linear possibilistic-probabilistic optimization problem with possibility or necessity constraints, LR fuzzy-random coefficients and weakest-t-norm dependence can be reduced to a stochastic programming analogue with center and spread terms.

The equivalent convex stochastic program can be attacked by a projected primal-dual stochastic quasigradient method using sample-based estimates instead of exactly computing expected spread functions.

For continuous convex objectives/constraints, a convex closed decision set, Slater feasibility, diminishing non-summable square-summable steps and the stated moment/normalization controls, an accumulation point belongs to the solution set almost surely.

Assuming finite second moments for the random scale variables is presented as a more easily checked sufficient condition for finite conditional squared quasigradient norms and a simplified almost-sure convergence theorem.

function_concept_used_by_paper: The paper uses functions in the mathematical-optimization sense, not software functions or probabilistic-program terms. A decision vector x is evaluated by linear fuzzy-random objective and constraint functions f_i(x, omega, gamma); expected LR center/spread functions are transformed into a stochastic Lagrangian; sampled quasigradient functions drive a projected primal-dual iteration.
representation_or_carrier: The carrier combines a probability space (Omega, B, P), a possibility space (Gamma, powerset(Gamma), pi), real decision vectors in a nonnegative subset X, and fuzzy random variables Y(omega,gamma). Coefficients have a shift-scale representation a(omega)+sigma(omega)Z(gamma), with Z an LR-type fuzzy quantity represented by left/right core and spread parameters. Possibilistic dependence is specified by a t-norm, specialized to the weakest t-norm T_W.
specification_language: A constrained mathematical program specifies an extremized auxiliary/objective value, possibility or necessity thresholds tau_i{E[f_i] relation_i k_i} >= alpha_i, and x in X. Linear fuzzy-random functions, LR shape functions L/R, expectation, independence, weakest-t-norm relatedness and convexity/Slater/moment/step-size assumptions complete the model. This is not a programming language and has no types, modules, pre/postconditions, executable syntax, API, provenance schema or general function contract.
compiler_or_generator: No compiler or generator is presented. The reduction from the hybrid possibilistic-probabilistic program to equations 3-4 is a hand-derived mathematical equivalence under a narrow linear LR/weakest-t-norm model. No automatic translator, symbolic checker or construction algorithm is implemented, and the paper does not measure the cost of forming or solving the analogue.
interpreter_or_runtime: The runtime analogue is an iterative projected stochastic quasigradient primal-dual optimizer: sample omega^s, construct xi^s and zeta^s for the Lagrangian, update x by projected descent and u by projected ascent with step rho_s gamma_s. The paper supplies formulas and convergence conditions but no code, pseudocode with stopping rules, parameter-selection procedure, numerical example, benchmark or executable artifact.
composition_rule: Expected values combine probabilistic randomness with LR fuzzy parameters, and t-norms aggregate possibilistic dependence. The Lagrangian composes one objective with multiplier-weighted constraints, while vector quasigradients sum the corresponding sample contributions. This is algebraic aggregation for one constrained optimization problem; the paper does not define compositional semantics for independently deployable stochastic functions or prove closure under general program/function composition.
state_or_effect_model: Iteration state is the primal-dual pair (x^s,u^s) plus its filtration/history B_s. Fresh sampled scale realizations determine stochastic quasigradients, and projections keep updates in X and U. No mutable software heap, event trace, concurrency, nondeterministic control flow, external I/O, checkpoint/restart or distributed state is modeled.
uncertainty_model: Aleatory uncertainty is represented by P over omega and possibilistic/fuzzy uncertainty by pi over gamma. A fuzzy random variable couples both; LR membership/possibility shapes and t-relatedness describe fuzziness and dependence, while expectation removes omega to produce a deterministic fuzzy expected value. The optimization constraints use possibility or necessity levels alpha. The method assumes known distributions/moments and does not estimate, calibrate or update them; it reports no finite-sample confidence bound, posterior, robustness analysis or sensitivity study.

validation_regime.proof_audit: the finite-moment conclusion is plausible and can be bounded using indicator <= 1 and Cauchy-Schwarz, but displayed conditional-expectation equalities pull sample-dependent maximizer indicators outside expectations; the transition from pointwise finite moments to the uniform control normally used by the inherited convergence theorem is not fully spelled out, and U is described as closed/convex rather than explicitly bounded
validation_regime.boundary: Theorem 3 is conditional on convexity, continuity, Slater feasibility, weakest-t-norm LR structure, finite second moments and Robbins-Monro step conditions; it establishes an almost-sure optimal accumulation point, not rate, full-sequence convergence or empirical performance

equivalence_notions.boundary: The paper cites the derivation to earlier work and does not extend it to nonlinear, non-LR or other t-norm settings.
The concrete construction is narrow, and no implementation test confirms the estimator identities.
This is weaker than whole-sequence convergence, has no rate, and the proof bridge from finite moments to uniform convergence control is compressed.
The displayed moment algebra treats sample-dependent indicators too casually and does not explicitly establish every uniform bound of Theorem 1.

limitations_and_failure_boundaries: Despite the English title's word programming, this is mathematical programming/optimization, not probabilistic programming-language semantics.
The optimization model is linear in x and assumes shift-scale LR fuzzy-random coefficients with mutually weakest-t-norm-related fuzzy components.
Convexity is noted for the necessity-measure parameterization; the method/theorem does not cover every possibility-measure relation or arbitrary nonconvex hybrid program.

Convergence requires continuous convex objective and constraints, a convex closed decision set, Slater feasibility, finite second moments, bounded normalization and diminishing steps with divergent sum and square-summable squares.
Theorem 3 guarantees only that one accumulation point is optimal almost surely, not uniqueness, full-sequence convergence, objective-gap convergence or a rate.

The displayed proof pulls maximizer indicators t_ij^s, which depend on the current random scale sample, outside conditional expectations; the needed finiteness can be recovered by inequalities but the printed equalities are not fully justified.

A cross-moment line factorizes conditional expectations of scale variables; this needs independence/fresh-sample conditions and is unnecessary if Cauchy-Schwarz is used, but the filtration assumptions are not developed carefully.
Pointwise finiteness of conditional moments is weaker than a uniform bound; the paper does not explicitly prove the uniform C_L bridge or require the dual projection set U to be bounded in Theorem 3.
No stopping criterion, finite-iteration error, sample complexity, computational complexity or numerical stability result is provided.
The conclusion explicitly leaves computational-complexity estimates and comparison with indirect solution methods to future work.
No numerical example, portfolio dataset, baseline comparison, sensitivity analysis or empirical convergence trace is reported.
The approach assumes the probability/possibility model, LR parameters, t-norm relationship and required moments are given; it does not learn or validate them from data.
There is no source code, solver artifact, reproducibility bundle or mechanized proof.
The journal/source is Russian-language with only an English abstract and references, limiting direct independent scrutiny for non-Russian readers.
The work does not address neural functions, general Function OS composition, ignition epsilon, frozen Psi_0 or governed artifact deployment.
what_the_paper_does_not_support: It does not provide a probabilistic programming language, stochastic-function interpreter or compositional program semantics.
It does not prove convergence for arbitrary fuzzy/probabilistic objectives, nonlinear programs, alternative dependence structures or unconstrained nonconvex settings.
It does not establish a convergence rate, finite-sample error, computational cost or superiority to deterministic/indirect methods.
It does not empirically validate the method on a portfolio or other real task.
It does not supply executable or reproducible solver artifacts, lifecycle governance, neural-function mappings or empirical validation of ignition.
